To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have produced the first covariant predictions for axial charges and axial currents of the nucleon, its resonant excitations and other hadrons.
the nucleon axial charge gA is 1.27 ±0.05, and the axial form factor is 0.27 ± 0.05 at Q2 = 0.5 GeV2 and 0.15 ±0.03 at Q2 =1 GeV2.
the axial charges of the nucleon as well as of its resonant excitations are well reproduced by our relativistic quark models.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the axial structure of nucleons and their excited states, and with the question of how the nucleons and N* resonates are built from their constituent quarks.
the structure of the nucleon as a relativistic bound state of quarks and gluons.
the axial properties of the nucleons and their excitations in the energy regime of the N* resonances.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the axial charges and axial currents are well understood within the relativistic constituent-quart picture.
the axial charges of the nucleon, its resonant states and their axial form factors are in good agreement with the predictions from the constituent-quark model.
the axial charge and axial form factor of all N* resonances can be calculated in relativistic constituent-quarks models.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
relativistic constituent-quarks models are able to reproduce the axial properties of the nucleons and N* resonant states with a good accuracy.
the axial current in the point-form relativistic quark model is a good approximation to the axial current in QCD.
relativistic covariant calculations of axial properties are possible in the point form.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the axial charge of the N*(1440) resonance is significantly smaller than that of the N*(1520) resonance.
relativistic constituent-quarks can be used as a tool to explore the properties of hadrons in a covariant framework.
the point-form relativistic quark models can be used to predict axial properties of hadrons with a precision that is comparable to that of lattice quantum chromodynamics.
